resources.title: Semantics derived automatically from language corpora contain human-like biases
resources.abstract: Machines learn what people know implicitly AlphaGo has demonstrated that a machine can learn how to do things that people spend many years of concentrated study learning, and it can rapidly learn how to do them better than any human can. Caliskan et al. now show that machines can learn word associations from written texts and that these associations mirror those learned by humans, as measured by the Implicit Association Test (IAT) (see the Perspective by Greenwald). Why does this matter? Because the IAT has predictive value in uncovering the association between concepts, such as pleasantness and flowers or unpleasantness and insects. It can also tease out attitudes and beliefs—for example, associations between female names and family or male names and career. Such biases may not be expressed explicitly, yet they can prove influential in behavior. Science , this issue p. 183 ; see also p. 133

resources.title: Bias Measurement — WEFE user guide
Man is to Computer Programmer as Woman is to Homemaker? Debiasing Word Embeddings
resources.abstract: The blind application of machine learning runs the risk of amplifying biases present in data. Such a danger is facing us with word embedding, a popular framework to represent text data as vectors which has been used in many machine learning and natural language processing tasks. We show that even word embeddings trained on Google News articles exhibit female/male gender stereotypes to a disturbing extent. This raises concerns because their widespread use, as we describe, often tends to amplify these biases. Geometrically, gender bias is first shown to be captured by a direction in the word embedding. Second, gender neutral words are shown to be linearly separable from gender definition words in the word embedding. Using these properties, we provide a methodology for modifying an embedding to remove gender stereotypes, such as the association between between the words receptionist and female, while maintaining desired associations such as between the words queen and female. We define metrics to quantify both direct and indirect gender biases in embeddings, and develop algorithms to "debias" the embedding. Using crowd-worker evaluation as well as standard benchmarks, we empirically demonstrate that our algorithms significantly reduce gender bias in embeddings while preserving the its useful properties such as the ability to cluster related concepts and to solve analogy tasks. The resulting embeddings can be used in applications without amplifying gender bias.

resources.title: Word embeddings quantify 100 years of gender and ethnic stereotypes
resources.abstract: Significance Word embeddings are a popular machine-learning method that represents each English word by a vector, such that the geometry between these vectors captures semantic relations between the corresponding words. We demonstrate that word embeddings can be used as a powerful tool to quantify historical trends and social change. As specific applications, we develop metrics based on word embeddings to characterize how gender stereotypes and attitudes toward ethnic minorities in the United States evolved during the 20th and 21st centuries starting from 1910. Our framework opens up a fruitful intersection between machine learning and quantitative social science.

resources.title: Image Representations Learned With Unsupervised Pre-Training Contain Human-like Biases
resources.abstract: Recent advances in machine learning leverage massive datasets of unlabeled images from the web to learn general-purpose image representations for tasks from image classification to face recognition. But do unsupervised computer vision models automatically learn implicit patterns and embed social biases that could have harmful downstream effects? We develop a novel method for quantifying biased associations between representations of social concepts and attributes in images. We find that state-of-the-art unsupervised models trained on ImageNet, a popular benchmark image dataset curated from internet images, automatically learn racial, gender, and intersectional biases. We replicate 8 previously documented human biases from social psychology, from the innocuous, as with insects and flowers, to the potentially harmful, as with race and gender. Our results closely match three hypotheses about intersectional bias from social psychology. For the first time in unsupervised computer vision, we also quantify implicit human biases about weight, disabilities, and several ethnicities. When compared with statistical patterns in online image datasets, our findings suggest that machine learning models can automatically learn bias from the way people are stereotypically portrayed on the web.

sample_claims.text: Association tests on the embeddings used by the CV-screening tool show no gender association between occupation terms and male or female terms above the effect size the team agreed to act on.

The clinical term embeddings in the diagnosis support model show no association between diagnosis terms and age or ethnicity terms above the agreed threshold, and the result holds with a second set of term lists.
Protected-characteristic terms do not sit systematically closer to creditworthiness terms than to their opposites in the lending model's text embeddings, under the word lists documented in the audit.

techniques.name: Few-Shot Fairness Evaluation
techniques.description: Few-shot fairness evaluation tests whether the worked examples placed in a prompt change how fairly a language model treats different demographic groups. The evaluator builds many versions of the same prompt, varying which examples appear and how each demographic group is represented among them. Each version is run on the same test inputs, and group-level results are compared across versions. Typical checks include the gap in outcomes between groups, whether outputs echo stereotypes present in the examples, and whether an input gets the same treatment when only a demographic term in it is swapped. The result shows how sensitive the model's fairness is to the choice of examples, and which compositions make outcomes more or less even.

example_use_cases.description: Testing whether a resume screening LLM's few-shot examples inadvertently introduce gender bias by showing more male examples for technical positions, affecting how it evaluates subsequent applicants.

Evaluating whether a medical triage LLM's few-shot examples for symptom assessment inadvertently encode demographic biases (e.g., more examples of cardiac symptoms in male patients), leading to differential urgency assessments across patient populations.

Assessing whether few-shot examples in a loan application review assistant systematically present more favourable examples for certain demographic profiles, biasing the model's assessment of creditworthiness for subsequent applications.

Testing whether an automated essay grading system keeps consistent standards across student demographics when its few-shot examples over-represent particular writing styles, dialects or cultural references.

limitations.description: The number of possible example sets, orderings and wordings is far too large to test exhaustively. The evaluation samples configurations and can miss the combinations that cause the worst disparities, so results describe what was tested rather than every prompt the system will meet.

Fairness measures can shift with small changes in example wording, order or prompt format, and with ordinary sampling variation in the model's replies. A gap between two example sets may be noise unless each is run repeatedly, and results seldom carry over to a different prompt template, instruction style or model version.

Needs test inputs labelled with demographic attributes, or pairs of inputs that differ only in a demographic term. These can be unavailable, costly to build or sensitive to hold, and they must reflect how the system will actually be prompted, which takes domain expertise to judge.

Each extra example set multiplies the number of model calls, because every set must be run on enough inputs for each group being compared. With large models and high inference costs, thorough coverage is expensive, which tempts teams to test fewer configurations.

resources.title: Fairness-guided few-shot prompting for large language models
resources.abstract: Large language models have demonstrated surprising ability to perform in-context learning, i.e., these models can be directly applied to solve numerous downstream tasks by conditioning on a prompt constructed by a few input-output examples. However, prior research has shown that in-context learning can suffer from high instability due to variations in training examples, example order, and prompt formats. Therefore, the construction of an appropriate prompt is essential for improving the performance of in-context learning. In this paper, we revisit this problem from the view of predictive bias. Specifically, we introduce a metric to evaluate the predictive bias of a fixed prompt against labels or a given attributes. Then we empirically show that prompts with higher bias always lead to unsatisfactory predictive quality. Based on this observation, we propose a novel search strategy based on the greedy search to identify the near-optimal prompt for improving the performance of in-context learning. We perform comprehensive experiments with state-of-the-art mainstream models such as GPT-3 on various downstream tasks. Our results indicate that our method can enhance the model's in-context learning performance in an effective and interpretable manner.

resources.title: Strategic Demonstration Selection for Improved Fairness in LLM In-Context Learning
resources.abstract: Recent studies highlight the effectiveness of using in-context learning (ICL) to steer large language models (LLMs) in processing tabular data, a challenging task given the structured nature of such data.Despite advancements in performance, the fairness implications of these methods are less understood.This study investigates how varying demonstrations within ICL prompts influence the fairness outcomes of LLMs.Our findings reveal that deliberately including minority group samples in prompts significantly boosts fairness without sacrificing predictive accuracy.Further experiments demonstrate that the proportion of minority to majority samples in demonstrations affects the trade-off between fairness and prediction accuracy.Based on these insights, we introduce a mitigation technique that employs clustering and evolutionary strategies to curate a diverse and representative sample set from the training data.This approach aims to enhance both predictive performance and fairness in ICL applications.Experimental results validate that our proposed method dramatically improves fairness across various metrics, showing its efficacy in real-world scenarios.

techniques.name: Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law Risk and Impact Assessment
techniques.description: HUDERIA is the Council of Europe's methodology for identifying and assessing the risks an AI system poses to human rights, democracy and the rule of law, and for planning how to prevent or reduce them, from design through deployment to retirement. It is non-binding guidance that public and private organisations may use or adapt in whole or in part; it was drawn up to support risk assessment in line with the Council of Europe's Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence, and the human rights treaties its resources cite are illustrative, binding only the states that are parties to them. A multidisciplinary team first runs a context-based risk analysis (COBRA): it scopes the system's purpose, data and affected groups, works through risk factors in the system's application, design and deployment contexts, maps potential impacts on specific rights and on democratic and legal processes, gives each impact an initial rating, and triages the system, deciding whether further assessment is needed and whether the system should be built or deployed at all. Impacts are rated for severity, judged by scale (how serious the harm is), scope (how many people, which groups and for how long) and reversibility (whether those affected can be restored to their earlier position), and for probability; for systems that may pose significant risks, the team may engage affected stakeholders and then re-examines and re-rates each impact in a fuller risk and impact assessment. The output is a mitigation plan that prefers avoiding a harm to reducing, repairing or compensating for it, names who is responsible for each measure, outlines where appropriate the remedies open to affected people, and schedules repeat reviews as the system and its context change.

example_use_cases.description: A city council's children's services department is offered a model that ranks safeguarding referrals for follow-up. A team of caseworkers, a data scientist and a human rights lawyer runs the context-based risk analysis, maps impacts on family life, non-discrimination and fair procedure, and at triage asks whether existing caseworker screening would serve the problem better and whether the referral data represent the families concerned, before deciding whether to procure the model at all.

A recruitment software company assessing a CV-screening model engages disabled and older job seekers, the groups its analysis found most exposed, then rates each mapped impact for scale, scope, reversibility and probability under a scoring rule it writes down. Its mitigation plan drops a feature that scored video interviews, an 'avoid' measure, rather than relying on correcting decisions afterwards, and names the owner of each remaining measure.

A national tax authority that assessed its fraud-risk model before launch repeats the risk and impact assessment when it adds bank-transaction data, and again when a change in benefit rules alters who is flagged. Each review updates the mitigation plan and the information and appeal routes offered to people wrongly flagged, so the assessment on file describes the system as it now runs.

A health ministry outside Europe adapts HUDERIA for a symptom-checker chatbot, keeping the treaty references in the risk-factor and impact lists only for the instruments its state is party to and adding its own constitution, health law and data protection law, while keeping the four elements and the severity variables so that its assessments follow a published structure others can recognise and check.

limitations.description: HUDERIA leaves the rule for combining scale, scope, reversibility and probability into a risk level, and the thresholds used at triage, to the authorities or project teams applying it. Two teams can rate the same system differently and both be following the methodology, so an assessment can be compared or checked only if the team records the scoring rule it chose and why.

Stakeholder engagement and the detailed risk and impact assessment are optional, and are expected mainly for systems that the team's own triage finds may pose significant risks. A team that under-rates a system at triage can skip the stages most likely to expose the problem, so the evidence is stronger when someone outside the team has reviewed the triage reasoning.

The assessment rests on documents, expert judgement and what stakeholders report; it does not test the system. Probability ratings made before a system is built can be little more than informed estimates, so claims about how the system actually behaves, for example whether it treats groups differently, need test results from other techniques alongside the assessment.

HUDERIA assesses one system at a time. It asks teams to consider cumulative effects when a system runs alongside others serving similar purposes, which is where many harms to democratic and legal processes arise, but gives no method for estimating them. An assessment can therefore find each system acceptable while their combined contribution to a wider harm goes unmeasured, so claims about societal impact need evidence beyond a single assessment.

A full assessment needs people who can judge impacts on rights in law as well as people who understand the system's data and design, and it is meant to be repeated over the system's life. Organisations without access to human rights legal expertise may be unable to carry out the impact mapping and mitigation planning to the depth the methodology intends.

techniques.name: AI Incident Reporting with the OECD Common Reporting Framework
techniques.description: AI incident reporting with the OECD common reporting framework records each event in which an AI system caused harm, or could plausibly have caused it, in the common set of 29 fields the OECD published in February 2025, so that reports from different organisations, sectors and countries can be compared and pooled. The framework is meant for both mandatory and voluntary reporting and defines what a report contains, not the reporting interface or what should happen afterwards. The reporter first classifies the event using the OECD's definitions: an AI incident is an event in which the development, use or malfunction of an AI system directly or indirectly leads to harm to people's health, disruption of critical infrastructure, a violation of human rights or of laws protecting fundamental, labour or intellectual property rights, or harm to property, communities or the environment, and an AI hazard is one that could plausibly lead to such harm. Seven fields are mandatory: a title, a description, how the AI system was involved (as a direct cause, a contributing factor, a failure to act, through over-reliance or misuse, through human error, or through a failure to comply with the law), who is reporting, supporting material, the severity (hazard, serious hazard, incident, serious incident or disaster) and the type of harm. The other 22 record, where known and among other things, when and where it happened, the system and the organisations behind it, the people affected, the sector, how widely the system was deployed, whether training data, the model or several interacting systems were involved, the system's task and level of autonomy, and any action taken, giving an inspectable register of what went wrong in operation.

example_use_cases.description: A retail bank's model risk team logs every complaint from customers or staff about its credit, fraud and customer-chatbot models that meets the OECD definition of an AI incident or hazard. A wrongly refused loan, an account frozen by a fraud alert and a chatbot quoting the wrong fees are recorded on the same severity scale and harm types, with the model and version and how the model was involved, so the quarterly risk committee can see which systems recur and which harms dominate.

A hospital records near misses as well as harms. When a radiologist notices that the imaging triage model has put an urgent scan at the back of the queue, the event is logged as an AI hazard, with the model's erroneous ranking as a direct cause, its autonomy recorded as human-in-the-loop, and the action taken, so that patterns of near misses are visible before one becomes an incident.

A national regulator that receives AI incident reports from deployers in several sectors asks for them in the OECD format, with a published note on how it judges seriousness, so that it can count serious incidents by sector and harm type and compare its figures with those of other authorities using the same fields.

A city transport authority running an AI traffic-signal optimiser records a period of emergency-vehicle delays as an incident affecting critical infrastructure, with the system as a contributing factor and an operator's configuration change as human error, so the record shows both causes and the follow-up actions assigned to the supplier and to its own staff.

limitations.description: A register is only as complete as the reports that reach it. Harms nobody notices, such as people quietly refused a service, and events staff have reasons not to report go unrecorded, so a short register is weak evidence that a system has caused little harm unless the organisation can also show how incidents are detected and how reporting is encouraged.

The OECD's own definitions say that seriousness is highly context-dependent, that each jurisdiction may define it differently, and that several small incidents can add up to a serious one. Two reporters can classify the same event differently, so counts of serious incidents can be compared only between reporters that share a written severity rule.

The framework standardises what is recorded, not how an incident is investigated or fixed, and the OECD paper explicitly gives no guidance on corrective or preventive action. Its field for how the AI system was involved is a short category list, and the fields on training data and the model are optional free text, so an organisation needs its own root-cause and follow-up process if records are to lead to changes.

None of the seven mandatory fields identifies the system or its version, the organisation that deployed it or the date of the event. Records kept to the mandatory minimum cannot trace incidents to a model release or show repeated failures of one system; the framework lets a reporting scheme make more fields mandatory, and an organisation that needs this traceability has to do so.

The framework is a recent proposal that the OECD planned to test through open submissions to its AI Incidents Monitor. Regulators that impose a legal duty to report incidents set their own format, categories and deadlines, so an organisation under such a duty reports in the regulator's format, may need to keep the OECD fields alongside, and cannot assume that an event serious on the OECD scale meets the legal definition of a serious incident, or the reverse.

techniques.name: SMACTR Internal Algorithmic Audit
techniques.description: SMACTR is an internal audit procedure for AI systems, proposed by Raji and colleagues in 2020, in which an audit team inside the developing organisation but separate from the product team examines a system during development and before launch against the ethical objectives and requirements the organisation has declared for it. The audit runs in five stages, each producing set documents. In Scoping, auditors review the product requirements and the declared objectives and write an ethical review of the use case, drawing in independent domain experts and marginalised groups, and a social impact assessment; in Mapping, they map the people involved, review existing design records, interview the engineers and begin a failure modes and effects analysis (FMEA), a systematic review of the foreseeable ways the system could fail and their effects, used to rank risks for testing. In Artefact Collection, a checklist confirms that the expected development documents, such as model cards and datasheets, exist; in Testing, auditors run tests chosen from the FMEA's priorities, such as adversarial probing with tailored inputs, and rate each risk high, mid or low from its likelihood and severity in an ethical risk analysis chart; in Reflection, they set the results against the declared objectives, finalise the risk analysis and agree a remediation plan with the engineering team. The documents are kept in an algorithmic design history file, from which the auditors write a summary report that leadership can use to decide whether the system launches, changes or is abandoned.

example_use_cases.description: An insurer's internal audit team audits a claims-triage model before launch. Interviews in Mapping reveal that a field used as a proxy for chronic illness was dropped late without the requirements being updated; the FMEA ranks under-prioritising complex claims as the top risk, so Testing concentrates on claims from people with several conditions, and the summary report goes to the risk committee with a remediation plan and a recommendation to delay launch.

A software company's responsible-AI audit team audits a customer-support chatbot. Artefact Collection finds no datasheet for the fine-tuning conversations, so the auditors require the product team to write one before testing; prompts drawn from the FMEA then test whether the bot discloses other customers' account details or gives poorer answers to customers writing in non-standard English, and the ethical risk chart and remediation plan record what must change before release.

A government digital service's audit team, which reports to the agency's chief risk officer rather than to the delivery programme, audits an in-house model that prioritises housing repair requests before it replaces manual triage. The chief risk officer uses the summary report to decide whether the model goes live, and the design history file and report are filed where the agency's external auditors and ombudsman can later inspect them.

limitations.description: The auditors are employees of the organisation they audit and share its interests; the authors acknowledge that independence is hard to keep and that audits risk becoming reputation management. Findings carry more weight when the audit team reports outside the product's management line and the design history file can be examined by an outside party.

The system is judged against the ethical objectives the organisation declares for it, which the authors note have been criticised as vague, and the paper leaves open what level of performance, for example how close to parity across groups, counts as acceptable. A clean audit shows consistency with the standards and thresholds the organisation chose to declare, and says nothing about any external standard it did not adopt.

The Testing stage prescribes no particular tests; the authors expect tests to vary widely by system and to follow the FMEA's priorities. What the audit can show about the system's behaviour therefore depends on the tests the team chooses, and a failure mode the FMEA did not foresee is likely to go untested.

The audit is deliberately slow and document-heavy, and the authors note that fast, iterative development is hard to audit. Its results describe the system at the time of the audit, so a model retrained or reconfigured afterwards is not covered unless the relevant stages are repeated.

The paper does not say which systems should be audited or in how much depth, leaving that to the organisation, and it illustrates the procedure only on two hypothetical client projects. Published evidence of how well it finds problems in real systems is limited.

techniques.name: Conditional Demographic Disparity
techniques.description: Conditional demographic disparity (CDD) measures whether members of a protected group make up a larger share of the people a system turns down than of the people it accepts, after taking into account a factor that differs between groups and that the assessor treats as a legitimate explanation of outcomes; Wachter, Mittelstadt and Russell (2021) propose it as baseline statistical evidence for assessing possible discrimination under EU non-discrimination law. Demographic disparity is the group's share of the unfavourable outcomes minus its share of the favourable ones: in the Berkeley graduate admissions data the paper revisits, women were 46 per cent of rejected applicants but 32 per cent of admitted ones, a disparity of 0.14. CDD computes the same difference separately within each stratum of the conditioning attribute (there, the department applied to) and averages the strata, weighting each by its number of people, so a gap that arises only because groups apply in different proportions to strata with different acceptance rates (an instance of Simpson's paradox) drops out, while a gap within strata remains. Conditioning on department turns the Berkeley figure to about -0.02, a slight disparity in women's favour: within departments, women were on average 40 per cent of rejected and 42 per cent of admitted applicants. The output is the disparity in each stratum and their weighted average, computed on the outcomes recorded in a dataset before training or on a model's decisions after it; the authors present it as a descriptive magnitude to support a contextual judgement, not a pass-or-fail test, and the choice of conditioning attribute is a judgement the measure does not make.

example_use_cases.description: An employer's HR analytics team audits a CV-screening model used across job families. Women make up a larger share of screened-out applicants than of shortlisted ones overall, but apply in greater numbers to the families with the fewest vacancies per applicant, so the team reports CDD conditioned on job family, with each family's own disparity, letting the recruitment board see whether a gap remains within families before it decides whether to keep using the model.

A consumer lender's compliance team computes CDD on its credit model's decisions for applicants of different ethnic origins, recorded for equality monitoring, conditioned first on the loan product applied for and then on income band. It reports both results with the per-stratum figures and a written reason for treating each factor as a legitimate explanation, as the starting point for its assessment of possible indirect discrimination.

A local authority planning to train a model on past housing allocation decisions measures CDD in those decisions, conditioned on assessed band of housing need, before any training. A positive disparity for one ethnic group within need bands, larger than chance would explain, indicates that the labels carry a pattern a model could learn, and the project board uses the finding to decide whether those decisions can serve as training labels at all.

limitations.description: The result depends on which attribute is conditioned on, and the measure cannot tell whether that attribute is a legitimate explanation. If the attribute is itself shaped by discrimination, for instance if one group was deterred from applying to some departments, conditioning on it removes the very disparity a claimant would point to. Wachter et al. leave the choice of factors to courts and context, so each choice needs a recorded justification that a reviewer can contest.

The weighted average can hide large disparities of opposite sign in different strata. In the Berkeley data the per-department disparities run from about -0.09 to +0.05 around a summary of -0.02, and Wachter et al. note that the largest swings come from the department where few women applied, which chance alone could produce. A claim should rest on the per-stratum figures, with their counts, as well as on the summary.

Searching many conditioning attributes or their combinations will find disparities by chance, as the authors warn, and choosing among them after seeing the results can equally make a real one disappear. The authors also offer a descriptive magnitude rather than a statistical test, and set no threshold for how much disparity is too much, so the conditioning attributes need fixing before the data are examined, and a claim that a gap is real needs an interval or test added.

CDD compares shares of outcomes, not rates, so the same gap in acceptance rates gives a smaller value where the group is a small part of a stratum: accepted at 20 per cent against 50 per cent for others, a group scores about 0.33 where it is half the stratum but 0.02 where it is 2 per cent. A fixed threshold therefore tolerates larger rate gaps for smaller groups. Scores and graded outcomes must also first be cut into favourable and unfavourable, and the result changes with the cut.

In the open-source SageMaker Clarify code, a stratum where everyone gets the same outcome is counted rather than skipped: an all-rejected stratum adds a disparity equal to the group's share of it, though no one there was treated differently, so such strata need removing first. AWS has closed Clarify to new customers. The calculation is easy to reimplement, but published applications to deployed AI systems are scarce; the paper's worked example is the 1975 Berkeley admissions study.

techniques.name: Disaggregated Evaluation
techniques.description: Disaggregated evaluation assesses and reports a system's performance separately for each group of people a claim covers, and for combinations of groups (intersectional groups, such as darker-skinned women), so that a good overall score cannot hide a group for whom the system works badly. Following Barocas et al. (2021), the evaluator first fixes the design choices that change what the evaluation can show: which groups and combinations to report; how other factors that affect performance, such as lighting or recording conditions, are handled (held constant, varied deliberately, or left as they occur); which metrics to use, for a classifier often false positive and false negative rates reported separately, because each can harm different people; and whether the evaluation is exploratory, or confirmatory, meaning that it tests hypotheses stated in advance on data built to hold enough cases in every group. Each metric is then computed on a labelled evaluation set for every group and combination, together with the number of cases behind it and an interval showing how far the estimate could move through sampling alone, obtained for example by resampling the evaluation set. Groups are compared by absolute and by relative gaps, which can tell different stories: false negative rates of 1 and 10 per cent differ by nine points but tenfold. The output is a table or chart of per-group and per-combination results with their case counts and intervals, and a record of the design choices needed to interpret them; it is this design, more than any one metric or interval method, that decides which comparisons the evaluation can support and how conclusive each is.

example_use_cases.description: Before a hospital trust adopts a supplier's skin-lesion classifier, its clinical safety team reports sensitivity and specificity on locally labelled images for each skin-tone group, sex and age band, and for skin tone crossed with sex. Cells holding fewer melanoma cases than the evaluation protocol requires are marked as too small to estimate rather than reported, and the trust collects more images for them before deciding whether the tool may be used for all patients.

A consumer organisation evaluating the speech-to-text services behind automated phone lines has speakers from several regional and ethnic groups, matched on age and gender, read identical scripted passages, and reports word error rate per group with intervals. Because everyone says the same words, a gap can be attributed to how each service recognises speech rather than to what was said, the evidence the organisation needs for a complaint to the providers.

A bank's model risk team runs a confirmatory evaluation of its fraud model each quarter. The groups (age band, sex and their combinations), the metrics (false positive rate, which drives blocked legitimate payments, and false negative rate), the sample and the largest acceptable gap are fixed in a protocol before the data are drawn, and the model stays in service only if every interval for a gap lies inside that margin.

An exam board piloting an automated essay-scoring model runs an exploratory evaluation of its agreement with human markers, split by first language, school type and their combinations. It finds one weak cell, candidates with English as an additional language at small schools, too small to be conclusive, and commissions a confirmatory study with a sample built to fill that cell before deciding whether the scores can count towards grades.

limitations.description: Each attribute added multiplies the number of cells and shrinks each one, so combinations of attributes soon hold too few cases for a stable estimate, and where a cell holds only a few errors, intervals from resampling come out too narrow. Comparing many cells also throws up some large gaps by chance. A confirmatory claim needs enough cases in every cell, which Barocas et al. note existing datasets rarely provide, so the data available limit which comparisons can be tested.

A gap between groups shows that performance differs, not why. Another factor that affects performance may differ between the groups, as with the time between paired images that NIST suggested could explain a higher false negative rate for Asian people in face recognition. Holding such a factor constant hides gaps at its other values, varying it needs the factor labelled for every case, and strongly correlated factors are hard to separate, or impossible when they always occur together.

The result is only as good as two sets of labels. Where ground-truth outcomes are wrong, or recorded differently for different groups, and the extent of the error cannot be identified, Barocas et al. note the results are meaningless however careful the design. Group membership is often ascribed by an institution or inferred from appearance, adding errors and possible harm to those labelled, and datasets may hold few of some groups (darker-skinned women were 4.4 per cent of one benchmark).

It measures differences in performance and nothing else. Equal error rates say nothing about whether outputs stereotype or demean people, or whether favourable decisions are shared in proportion, and narrowing a gap under one metric can open a gap under another. A clean result supports a claim about the performance gaps measured, for the groups and conditions tested, and no wider fairness claim.

Results on a laboratory dataset may not carry over to the system in use, where lighting, recording conditions and operators' decisions differ, and Barocas et al. note that a component's performance alone may say little about the whole system around it. Evaluating in the setting of use captures this but is costly, and is often impossible for an outside evaluator, who usually sees the system only as a black box.

resources.abstract: Recent studies demonstrate that machine learning algorithms can discriminate based on classes like race and gender. In this work, we present an approach to evaluate bias present in automated facial analysis algorithms and datasets with respect to phenotypic subgroups. Using the dermatologist  approved Fitzpatrick Skin Type classification system, we characterize the gender and skin type distribution of two facial analysis benchmarks, IJB-A and Adience. We find that these datasets are overwhelmingly composed of lighter-skinned subjects (79.6% for IJB-A and 86.2% for Adience) and introduce a new facial analysis dataset which is balanced by gender and skin type. We evaluate 3 commercial gender classification systems using our dataset and show that darker-skinned females are the most misclassified group (with error rates of up to 34.7%). The maximum error rate for lighter-skinned males is 0.8%. The substantial disparities in the accuracy of classifying darker females, lighter females, darker males, and lighter males in gender classification systems require urgent attention if commercial companies are to build genuinely fair, transparent and accountable facial analysis algorithms.

techniques.name: Predictive Parity and Calibration Within Groups
techniques.description: This test checks whether a model's output means the same for every group: among people who receive the same score or the same decision, the share who turn out to have the outcome (or its average, for an outcome such as a cost or a count of illnesses) should not depend on their group, a requirement the fairness literature calls sufficiency. For a model that outputs a risk score, cases with known outcomes are grouped into score bins and, for each group, the observed outcome rate in each bin is plotted against the score, giving one calibration curve per group (a score is calibrated when, of the cases scored 0.3, about 30 per cent have the outcome); calibration within groups (Kleinberg, Mullainathan and Raghavan) holds when each group's curve matches the scores, and the weaker condition that the curves coincide holds when a given score corresponds to the same outcome rate in every group. For a yes/no decision the same comparison is made in the two cells of the decision: predictive parity (Chouldechova) holds when the positive predictive value, the share of people flagged positive who turn out positive, is equal across groups, and the negative predictive value can be compared in the same way for those not flagged. The two read-outs can disagree, because a score that means the same for every group can still give unequal positive predictive values at a threshold when the groups' scores are spread differently above it, so the test reports the read-out matching the output on which decisions are taken, with intervals and the gaps between groups. Where comparisons of error rates condition on the true outcome and ask whether people who turn out the same are treated the same, this test conditions on the model's output and asks whether people treated the same turn out the same; when the outcome is more common in one group, the two cannot both hold except in special cases.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital's clinical informatics team checks a deterioration-risk score before it is shown to ward staff. On a year of admissions with recorded outcomes it plots a calibration curve, with intervals, for each ethnic group and each sex, and approves the score for use with every patient only if, across the scores that trigger escalation, each group's curve stays within a band agreed with clinicians.

A lender's model validation team compares the repayment rate among approved applicants across age bands, using two years of outcomes, to check whether approval means the same for each band. Because a difference among the approved can come from how scores are spread above the cut-off rather than from a different bar for one band, it also compares the calibration curves of the underlying score before raising any finding with the credit risk committee.

A probation service assessing a supplier's reoffending-risk tool is shown evidence that its positive predictive value is equal across ethnic groups. Its analysts reproduce the figures on local data and set them beside the groups' false positive and false negative rates, which differ because reconviction rates differ, so that the oversight board chooses which criterion the tool will be held to with both sets of figures in front of it.

A health insurer auditing a score that selects members for a care-management programme checks twice whether the score means the same for every racial group: against next year's costs, the label the model was trained on, and against a measure of illness such as the number of active chronic conditions. A score calibrated for cost but not for illness, with one group sicker than another at the same score, would lead the insurer to retrain on a different label.

limitations.description: When the outcome is more common in one group, a score or decision that satisfies predictive parity cannot also give the groups both equal false positive and equal false negative rates, and calibration within groups cannot coexist with equal average scores for each group's positives and negatives except with perfect prediction or equal base rates (Chouldechova; Kleinberg et al.). Passing this test therefore means accepting unequal error rates, a choice the test informs but cannot make.

Passing says little about how accurately the model predicts for each group. A well-fitted model usually comes close to calibration within groups without any fairness intervention when group membership can be inferred from its inputs, and a model that predicts accurately for one group while giving everyone in another group that group's average rate is still perfectly calibrated (Barocas, Hardt and Narayanan). The result needs pairing with performance measured for each group.

The test uses recorded outcomes, so it inherits any difference between groups in how the outcome is recorded. Rearrest stands in for reoffending, and a care-management score was calibrated by race for health costs while, at the 97th percentile of the score, Black patients had 26 per cent more chronic illnesses than white patients (Obermeyer et al.). A model can pass while scoring one group's need too low, so the outcome tested must be the one the claim is about.

A gap in positive predictive value is not by itself evidence that the score treats groups differently: the value averages over everyone above the threshold, so it depends on how each group's scores are spread there and moves when the threshold moves. Chouldechova notes that well-calibrated scores can fail predictive parity, and the converse also holds. Where scores are available the calibration curves should be reported, and the threshold stated.

Per-group calibration curves need labelled cases across the score range in every group; in a small group the high-score bins may hold a handful of people, so their rates swing widely, and the choice of bin widths changes the picture. An outside auditor who sees only decisions, not scores, can test predictive parity but not calibration, so access determines which claim the evidence can support.

resources.abstract: Malnutrition is a frequently underdiagnosed condition leading to increased morbidity, mortality, and healthcare costs. The Mount Sinai Health System (MSHS) deployed a machine learning model (MUST-Plus) to detect malnutrition upon hospital admission. However, in diverse patient groups, a poorly calibrated model may lead to misdiagnosis, exacerbating health care disparities. We explored the model’s calibration across different variables and methods to improve calibration. Data from adult patients admitted to five MSHS hospitals from January 1, 2021 - December 31, 2022, were analyzed. We compared MUST-Plus prediction to the registered dietitian’s formal assessment. Hierarchical calibration was assessed and compared between the recalibration sample (N = 49,562) of patients admitted between January 1, 2021 - December 31, 2022, and the hold-out sample (N = 17,278) of patients admitted between January 1, 2023 - September 30, 2023. Statistical differences in calibration metrics were tested using bootstrapping with replacement. Before recalibration, the overall model calibration intercept was −1.17 (95% CI: −1.20, −1.14), slope was 1.37 (95% CI: 1.34, 1.40), and Brier score was 0.26 (95% CI: 0.25, 0.26). Both weak and moderate measures of calibration were significantly different between White and Black patients and between male and female patients. Logistic recalibration significantly improved calibration of the model across race and gender in the hold-out sample. The original MUST-Plus model showed significant differences in calibration between White vs. Black patients. It also overestimated malnutrition in females compared to males. Logistic recalibration effectively reduced miscalibration across all patient subgroups. Continual monitoring and timely recalibration can improve model accuracy.

sample_claims.text: Across the deterioration-risk scores that trigger escalation, each ethnic group's observed deterioration rate lies within 3 percentage points of the rate for all patients with the same score, with the 95 per cent interval for each gap inside that band, on twelve months of admissions held out from model development.

Among applicants approved by the credit model in the evaluation period, the repayment rate for each age band is within 2 percentage points of the rate for all approved applicants, and the calibration curves of the underlying score for each band are reported alongside.

At the deployed threshold, the reoffending-risk tool's positive predictive value differs between ethnic groups by less than 5 percentage points on local data, and the corresponding differences in false positive and false negative rates are reported with it.

At each decile of the care-management score, the mean number of active chronic conditions differs between racial groups by less than the tolerance agreed with the clinical lead, so the score indicates the same level of illness in every group, not only the same expected cost.

techniques.name: Bias Benchmark for Question Answering
techniques.description: The Bias Benchmark for Question Answering (BBQ) is a fixed set of about 58,500 multiple-choice reading questions that tests whether a language model's answers rely on social stereotypes, across nine social dimensions (age, disability status, gender identity, nationality, physical appearance, race and ethnicity, religion, socio-economic status and sexual orientation) and two combinations of them, using stereotypes documented as harmful in US English-speaking contexts (Parrish et al., 2022). Each item describes two people from different groups and asks a question that points at a stereotype, such as who is bad at maths, with three answers to choose from: either person, or an answer such as 'cannot be determined'; in the ambiguous version the passage does not say which person the question is about, so 'cannot be determined' is correct, and in the disambiguated version an added sentence settles it. Items come in balanced sets that swap the two groups and their order and pair each negative question with a non-negative one, so that a model which simply prefers one group whatever the question is not counted as stereotyping. From the model's chosen answers (generated, or picked by comparing the probabilities it gives the three options) the test reports accuracy in each version and a bias score per category from -100% to 100%: the share of answers naming a person that follow the stereotype, rescaled so that 0 means no consistent direction and a negative score leans against the stereotype, and in the ambiguous version multiplied by the error rate, so that stereotyped guesses weigh more when the model guesses often; it also reports how far accuracy falls when the correct answer goes against the stereotype. Unlike substituting identity terms into a deployer's own inputs, or varying the people shown in few-shot examples, BBQ is a fixed external question set that tests what a model concludes about people when the text does, and does not, support a conclusion.

example_use_cases.description: A government department choosing between three language models for a service that answers citizens' questions about benefits runs the full BBQ set on each, with the same prompt, answer extraction and scoring for all three. It compares accuracy and both bias scores category by category, rules out any model whose ambiguous-context bias score in any category is further from zero, in either direction, than a limit set before testing, and records that the result covers US stereotypes only.

A recruitment software company fine-tuning an open-weight model to answer HR helpdesk questions runs BBQ on the base model and on every fine-tuned version through the same evaluation harness, logging each answer. A release is blocked if any category's ambiguous-context bias score moves further from zero than the base model's by more than an agreed margin, or if the accuracy gap between items whose correct answer matches the stereotype and items whose correct answer goes against it widens.

An NHS trust's digital team preparing a health-information assistant needs evidence about UK stereotypes, which BBQ was not built for. Following the procedure used to build a Korean version, it keeps templates that transfer, changes target groups where UK stereotypes differ, drops those that do not apply, writes UK-specific ones, surveys members of the UK public to confirm each stereotype and its target group, and reports results on the original and adapted sets side by side.

limitations.description: BBQ's stereotypes, and most of its categories, come from US English-speaking contexts, and its authors say results should not be used as evidence about other cultures. Adapting it to Korean meant changing target groups, dropping templates and adding four categories, and a machine-translated BBQ gave different bias scores from the adapted version (Jin et al., 2024). For a UK deployment the original set says nothing about UK-specific stereotypes.

A low bias score is weak evidence that a model is unbiased. Each category rests on about 25 templates with very short passages and three fixed answers; the authors warn that a low score is not proof of an unbiased model, and that for a model used on very different text BBQ is unlikely to be a valid measure. It counts only stereotypes that change the chosen answer, so it misses bias that shifts the model's probabilities without changing its choice.

The bias score leaves out 'cannot be determined' answers and has a sign, so it must be read with accuracy and by its distance from zero. A model that always gives that answer has full accuracy and a zero bias score on ambiguous items, yet fails every disambiguated one. A negative score means answers lean against the stereotype, as HELM found for most of the models it tested (Liang et al., 2023); a one-sided limit such as 'below 5%' passes such a model.

Scores depend on the prompt format and on how answers are extracted or scored, so they compare only across models tested the same way. In the original study one UnifiedQA model, given the same items in two input formats, scored 2.4 and 18.6 on ambiguous gender-identity items. Results for a single template rest on few items (one reported example has 72), so they are noisy and should be combined across templates for the same stereotype.

It is weak evidence about bias against people with two combined identities. In the original study, results on the two intersectional categories (race by gender, race by socio-economic status) were too inconsistent for the authors to conclude that models responded to more than one aspect of identity, and the lm-evaluation-harness task notes that these categories are not really taken into account in its bias scores.

resources.abstract: Language models (LMs) are becoming the foundation for almost all major language technologies, but their capabilities, limitations, and risks are not well understood. We present Holistic Evaluation of Language Models (HELM) to improve the transparency of language models. First, we taxonomize the vast space of potential scenarios (i.e. use cases) and metrics (i.e. desiderata) that are of interest for LMs. Then we select a broad subset based on coverage and feasibility, noting what's missing or underrepresented (e.g. question answering for neglected English dialects, metrics for trustworthiness). Second, we adopt a multi-metric approach: We measure 7 metrics (accuracy, calibration, robustness, fairness, bias, toxicity, and efficiency) for each of 16 core scenarios when possible (87.5% of the time). This ensures metrics beyond accuracy don't fall to the wayside, and that trade-offs are clearly exposed. We also perform 7 targeted evaluations, based on 26 targeted scenarios, to analyze specific aspects (e.g. reasoning, disinformation). Third, we conduct a large-scale evaluation of 30 prominent language models (spanning open, limited-access, and closed models) on all 42 scenarios, 21 of which were not previously used in mainstream LM evaluation. Prior to HELM, models on average were evaluated on just 17.9% of the core HELM scenarios, with some prominent models not sharing a single scenario in common. We improve this to 96.0%: now all 30 models have been densely benchmarked on the same core scenarios and metrics under standardized conditions. Our evaluation surfaces 25 top-level findings. For full transparency, we release all raw model prompts and completions publicly for further analysis, as well as a general modular toolkit. We intend for HELM to be a living benchmark for the community, continuously updated with new scenarios, metrics, and models.

No fine-tuned release of the HR helpdesk model has an ambiguous-context BBQ bias score more than 2 percentage points further from zero than the base model's in any category, measured with the same harness version, prompt and scoring.

On a UK-adapted version of BBQ, whose stereotypes and target groups were confirmed by a survey of the UK public before use, the health-information assistant's ambiguous-context bias score was between -5% and +5% in every category and its accuracy on disambiguated items was above 90%.

techniques.name: Rich Subgroup Fairness Auditing
techniques.description: Rich subgroup fairness auditing checks whether a binary classifier treats any subgroup much better or much worse than the population as a whole, where the subgroups are not a short list chosen in advance but every group that rules of a chosen kind over several protected attributes can describe, such as everyone for whom a weighted sum of age, sex and ethnicity indicators exceeds a threshold. Kearns, Neel, Roth and Wu (2018) proposed it to detect what they call fairness gerrymandering: a classifier can have equal false positive rates for men and for women, and for each ethnic group, yet very unequal rates for particular combinations, such as women of one ethnicity. For a chosen rate (the false positive or false negative rate, or in the paper also the rate of positive decisions), each subgroup is scored by the gap between its rate and the overall rate multiplied by the share of all records that are in the subgroup and count towards that rate (for the false positive rate, those with a negative true outcome), so a gap counts for more the larger the group, and the audit searches for the subgroup with the highest score. Exact search is computationally hard in the worst case, so it is posed as a weighted (cost-sensitive) classification problem over the protected attributes and solved approximately: the reference implementation fits two linear regressions that propose a candidate worst subgroup as a linear threshold rule, using only those attributes, the true outcomes and the classifier's decisions, not the model itself. The output is that rule with the subgroup's size, rate and weighted gap (called gamma), compared with a limit set beforehand; unlike reporting metrics for groups listed in advance, the audit finds subgroups nobody listed, and unlike multiaccuracy boosting, which checks a score's average error in each subgroup and then corrects the model, it compares a decision rate with the overall rate and changes nothing.

example_use_cases.description: A lender's model risk team validating a credit-risk model before release audits its decisions on a held-out sample of past applicants whose repayment is known, and records that these are only applicants the old policy approved. It searches subgroups over age, sex, ethnicity and disability status for the worst false positive rate gap (good payers flagged as high risk), compares it with a limit agreed with the risk committee, and sends the rule for any subgroup over it to the developers.

A hospital's clinical AI team has confirmed that a sepsis early-warning model misses cases at similar rates for men and women and for each recorded ethnic group. Before rollout it audits the false negative rate over subgroups combining age, sex and ethnicity and, because the search is approximate, also scores a grid of rules over two of the attributes by brute force, as the method's authors did, to check the search did not miss a larger gap.

A local authority's internal audit team re-audits a model that flags housing benefit claims for fraud review each quarter, using a random sample of claims reviewed whether or not they were flagged. It records the worst subgroup by false positive rate (legitimate claims flagged) over age, sex, ethnicity and disability, with its size and gap, and escalates to the system owner when the weighted gap exceeds the agreed limit.

limitations.description: Finding the worst subgroup exactly is hard in the worst case, even for conjunctions or linear thresholds of attributes (Kearns et al. 2018, Theorem 3.3), so practical audits use a heuristic search. A subgroup it reports does have the measured gap on the audit data, but a clean result is only a lower bound: the authors note their auditor could miss a larger disparity and checked it by brute force on two attributes (Kearns et al. 2019). 'Nothing found' is a search result, not a proof.

Gaps are weighted by subgroup size, which the authors require for reliable estimates and which lets small groups pass with large gaps: a subgroup holding 2% of the records whose false positive rate is 20 percentage points above the overall rate scores at most 0.004, under the 0.005 limit used in the AIF360 demonstration. The audit cannot support a claim about a small named group; report that group's own rate, with an interval, instead.

Only subgroups that the rule class can describe, over the attributes designated as protected, are searched; the reference implementation uses linear threshold rules. The class has to be limited because, as the authors note, any imperfect classifier could be accused of unfairness to the set of people it misclassifies. A protected attribute that is not recorded or not designated is invisible, so the attributes used and their encoding must be stated with the finding.

Error-rate audits need the protected attributes and the true outcome for every audited record, which a deployed system may not supply, for example when outcomes are seen only for approved applications. Reliable estimates need more data the richer the subgroup class, the authors' experiments report in-sample results, and the tools give no confidence interval, so audit on held-out data and repeat on fresh data before relying on a worst-case figure.

It tests parity of one rate at a time for binary decisions, each subgroup's rate against the overall rate. A pass on false positives says nothing about false negatives, the AIF360 auditor implements only those two error rates, and other criteria, such as whether scores mean the same in every subgroup (calibration), need a different test. The rate must be chosen to match the fairness claim before the audit.

resources.title: Preventing Fairness Gerrymandering: Auditing and Learning for Subgroup Fairness
resources.abstract: The most prevalent notions of fairness in machine learning fix a small collection of pre-defined groups (such as race or gender), and then ask for approximate parity of some statistic of the classifier (such as false positive rate) across these groups. Constraints of this form are susceptible to fairness gerrymandering, in which a classifier is fair on each individual group, but badly violates the fairness constraint on structured subgroups, such as certain combinations of protected attribute values. We thus consider fairness across exponentially or infinitely many subgroups, defined by a structured class of functions over the protected attributes. We first prove that the problem of auditing subgroup fairness for both equality of false positive rates and statistical parity is computationally equivalent to the problem of weak agnostic learning — which means it is hard in the worst case, even for simple structured subclasses. However, it also suggests that common heuristics for learning can be applied to successfully solve the auditing problem in practice. We then derive an algorithm that provably converges in a polynomial number of steps to the best subgroup-fair distribution over classifiers, given access to an oracle which can solve the agnostic learning problem. The algorithm is based on a formulation of subgroup fairness as a zero-sum game between a Learner (the primal player) and an Auditor (the dual player). We implement a variant of this algorithm using heuristic oracles, and show that we can effectively both audit and learn fair classifiers on a real dataset.

techniques.name: Actionable Recourse Audit
techniques.description: An actionable recourse audit checks whether the people a linear classifier refuses, for example for a loan, a job interview or a public service, could change that decision through actions open to them, and how much they would have to change. The auditor first writes an action set saying which features can change and how: immutable features such as age stay fixed, features such as education level can only rise, and each changeable feature gets bounds and a grid of realistic values. Then, for each refused person in a sample drawn from the population the model will serve, an integer programming solver (optimisation software that searches discrete choices exactly) looks through the permitted actions for the cheapest change that flips the decision, measuring cost as the largest shift, in population percentiles, that the change makes to any one feature, and either returns that action or proves that none exists, which a search that simply fails to find a counterfactual cannot do. The audit reports the share of refused people who have recourse and the distribution of its cost, which can be compared across candidate models or broken down by group, and the same solver can list a refused person's cheapest alternative changes (a 'flipset') for a decision notice. Unlike the Contrastive Explanation Method, which explains one prediction through features that must be present or absent, or Diverse Counterfactual Explanations (DiCE), which searches any model for several alternative inputs that would change one decision, the audit works only on linear models but certifies whether any permitted action exists and summarises the answer across a population.

example_use_cases.description: Before launching a linear model that ranks applications to a housing support scheme, a local authority's analytics team audits recourse on last year's applicants, with age and household size fixed. Its report to the scheme's oversight board gives the share of refused applicants who could qualify through changes the scheme expects, such as completing a tenancy course, and how large those changes are, so the board can decide whether to approve the model.

A credit card issuer generates a flipset for each applicant its linear scorecard declines and puts the two cheapest items in the decline letter, for example reducing current debt to a stated amount, together with the other scored features the applicant should keep unchanged, so that following the stated actions would change the decision under the current model.

A lender's model risk committee is shown recourse audits for candidate credit models of almost equal accuracy. It rejects the most accurate, under which some refused applicants had no feasible action because of an 'ever defaulted' feature, adopts a variant that uses recent defaults only, and has the audit re-run each quarter on new applicants, watching younger applicants, who were scarce in the training data.

An employer's analytics team audits its linear screening model for interview invitations and compares the cost of recourse for refused women and men with similar predicted scores. Sex is not a model input, but the cost can still differ by sex. Refused candidates' true suitability is never observed, so the team cannot also match on outcome as the originating study did, and reports any gap with that caveat to its fairness review panel, which decides whether the features need revising.

limitations.description: The proof that no action exists depends on the model being linear, such as logistic regression, a linear support vector machine or a rule set that can be written in linear form. For tree ensembles or neural networks, a local linear approximation can still suggest actions, which then have to be checked on the real model, but a failure to find one proves nothing, so the share of refused people without recourse is no longer a certified figure.

Every conclusion rests on the action set and cost the auditor chooses. Bounds that are too tight make people appear to lack recourse; loose bounds let a model 'provide' recourse only through drastic changes, which shows only as high cost; and the default cost treats a one-percentile change as equally hard in every feature unless someone who knows the domain sets how much harder some changes are.

The search treats features as changing independently unless the auditor adds constraints. Real actions have knock-on effects: raising income can also raise savings, so a listed action may cost more than needed, or may not change the decision once its effects on other features are counted, as Karimi, Schölkopf and Valera showed for recourse methods that ignore causal relations between features.

Recourse is defined for a fixed model. After retraining, an action given in an earlier notice may no longer change the decision, so the audit has to be re-run after each update. An action that changes the prediction need not change the real outcome either: showing a refused applicant how to be approved can lead them into credit they cannot repay.

A flipset lists only the features to change, so a person who also changes an undisclosed feature may still be refused unless the notice says what must stay the same. The originating paper builds flipsets from public credit datasets and does not test whether refused people understand them or can act on them. Owners may also resist publishing flipsets, because many of them together can let others reconstruct the model.
